text: You already built real workloads against the Kubernetes API back in course nine — Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, Secrets. This lesson asks a sharper question: exactly which part of that is portable across AKS, EKS, and an on-prem cluster, and which part only looks like it is? Getting that boundary right is the whole game in multi-cloud architecture, because getting it wrong means discovering the hard way, in production, that something you assumed traveled with the manifest actually didn't.

Here's the real mechanism: Kubernetes conformance testing guarantees that core object kinds — Deployment, Service, ConfigMap, Secret, PersistentVolumeClaim — behave identically on every CNCF-conformant distribution. Run kubectl apply against the exact same manifest on an AKS node pool, an EKS node group, or a Rancher-managed cluster on your own hardware, and you get the same rolling-update behavior, the same readiness-probe handling, the same label-selector matching. The object you declare is the unit of portability. The cluster underneath it, and the cloud account it happens to sit in, are not.

But that portability has a hard edge, hidden inside fields that look perfectly generic. Set type: LoadBalancer on a Service, and a cloud controller manager — different software per provider — provisions a real load balancer: an Azure Load Balancer here, an AWS NLB there, nothing at all on bare metal without an add-on. StorageClass names aren't standardized either — managed-csi on AKS, gp3 or ebs-sc on EKS — so a claim that binds on one cluster can fail outright on another. Ingress annotations only mean something to the specific controller installed. And how a pod gets cloud credentials sits entirely outside the Kubernetes API.

Look at a real Deployment and Service pair and you can point to exactly where that line falls. Replica count, container image, readiness probe, label selectors — none of that names a cloud. The moment you add type: LoadBalancer or reference a StorageClass by name, you've stepped outside the conformant core and into provider-specific territory, managed deliberately with a small, explicit set of per-cloud overlays rather than papered over and hoped to travel unchanged.

So the practical rule is simple to state and easy to forget under deadline pressure: treat the workload-definition layer as your genuinely portable core, and treat load-balancer provisioning, storage-class names, and ingress-controller behavior as an environment-specific overlay you own on purpose. Next lesson pushes that same discipline one layer up the stack — into the actual cloud services, like message queues and managed databases, that your workload talks to once it's running.
